subject: 👻 9 scary charts!

96 
Plus: Haunted housing | Friday, October 30, 2026
   
 
 View in browser 
   
 
   
 Axios Markets By
Emily Peck and Matt Phillips
 · 
Oct 30, 2026
 
 
 🎃 Friday! And tomorrow's Halloween. We're looking forward to eating even more candy — especially those delightful Reese's Peanut Butter Pumpkins — thanks to that extra hour we get on Sunday when we set the clocks back.

 🗓️ Today is looking like another rough session for the AI trade, with Amazon down sharply after yesterday's weaker-than-expected Q3 earnings report. 

 And Intel is diving, down roughly 25% in the premarket session after issuing an ugly Q4 outlook as part of its earnings report. 👻 We have treats for you, too! A real chart-a-palooza featuring some of the scariest charts Matt could cook up, plus Emily looks at the haunted housing market. 

 Let's go — if you dare! In 1,134 words, a 4.5-minute read. 


 
   
   
 
1 big thing: The haunted housing market
 
 By Emily Peck 
   
 
 
 
 Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios


 
   
 
 Here's a scary truth: The housing market is haunted. Home sales are anemic, yet prices are still high, and homebuilders say it's hard getting people out to even look at places.

 Why it matters: For a long time, the residential real estate market was a crucial economic engine in the U.S., and homeownership the backbone of the American dream and wealth building. 

 Now, not so much. Where it stands: The average rate on the 30-year mortgage is 7.24%, up from just under 6% at the start of the Iran war — that put the kibosh on what had been a tentative thaw in the frozen sector.

 With rates that high, a lot of folks — particularly younger first-time buyers — can't afford the monthly payments. In September, 14.5% of pending home sales fell out of contract, per Redfin , the highest share outside the early pandemic. Traffic of prospective buyers to new homes fell to its lowest level since 2012 this month, according to a survey of homebuilders from the National Association of Home Builders. Data: NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios The big picture: This is a situation years in the making. After the financial crisis in 2008, the Federal Reserve kept interest rates ultra-low, which meant low mortgage rates for buyers.

 Perhaps, perversely, that helped drive up home prices — you can afford to pay more when your mortgage rate is low. Home prices exploded, culminating in around a 40% increase during the 2021 and 2022 buying frenzy. State of play: But now, home prices are still high — they haven't adjusted down as mortgage rates have gone back up.

 Catch up quick: The previous era's low mortgage rates — an average of 4.15% from 2008-2021 — were an anomaly. 

 "Consequently, there is little reason to believe that mortgage rates will fall much below 7.0% in the months or even years ahead, in the absence of a recession," David Kelly, chief global strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management, wrote in a note titled, yes, "Haunted Housing." Zoom out: The situation is increasingly putting homeownership out of reach for young adults — the homeownership rate for that group, which had bounced back from its post-pandemic low, has fallen back some in recent years. 

 Kelly says this is the scariest chart of all: Data: U.S. Census Bureau, JPMorgan Asset Management; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios The bottom line: The housing market is more trick than treat lately.


 
 
   
   
 
2. Alphabet suffers a rough day for the ages
 
 By Matt Phillips 
   
 
 Data: FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips Yesterday was a day that will live in infamy for Alphabet shareholders, as the stock plunged 12.6%, vaporizing more than half a trillion dollars in value. 

 Why it matters: The massive one-day loss shows how AI continues to cause violent bouts of uncertainty throughout the markets, even for giants like Alphabet that have been considered big winners of the AI buildout. 

 Catch up quick: Alphabet's plunge followed lackluster third-quarter results posted Wednesday afternoon that seemed to suddenly raise questions not only about the extent of the company's spending on AI, but also about the durability of its core search advertising business. 

 What they're saying: Alphabet faces "unresolved if not intensifying competition risk from GenAI search products, including a potential Muse/Meta AI search product, as well as the threat of share loss to GenAI challengers," UBS analysts wrote in a note yesterday. 

 The bottom line: AI giveth and AI taketh away. 


 
 
   
   
A MESSAGE FROM AXIOS

🔒 Get the report by becoming a Media Trends Executive member.


 
   
   
 
3. 🦇 Some of the spookiest charts we see right now
 
 By Matt Phillips 
   
 
 Data: FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips It's natural to be jumpy this time of year, with armies of undead pedestrians hitting the streets tomorrow in search of moist human brain — and Skittles. 

 To add to the mood, here are some of the charts we've seen recently that have made the hair on our arms stand up. Why it matters: After weeks of wobbling sideways, the markets seem to be at a crossroads amid real questions about the durability of the AI trade and the economic boom that backs it. 

 Were the AI boom to suddenly turn to bust, it could have scary implications for the economy — investment in data centers is supercharging GDP — the markets and the finances of investors. The big picture: The stock market has become increasingly AI-pilled, with tech stocks and hyperscalers now accounting for more than half the capitalization of the S&P 500. This is higher even than during the dot-com-driven market boom that peaked in early 2000, before the market crashed. 

 Context: American households are long in the market, as they've never been before. 

 Data: Federal Reserve; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips Zoom in: At the same time, there are real questions emerging about the durability of the AI boom.

 For instance, prices for tokens — the main measure of AI computing power usage — are tumbling. That's not something you typically see in a market where demand is off the charts, which AI insiders claim. Data: Ramp; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips Between the lines: Falling prices don't mean sales won't go up. (If you boost volumes because of lower prices, you can still make more revenue.) 

 But it will sure make it harder to generate the revenue to pay off the massive amounts of debt that tech companies have sunk into AI. The market is increasingly scrutinizing companies considered the weakest financial links in the AI ecosystem. Case in point: The corporate bond market sharply repriced the interest rates it thinks CoreWeave should pay in recent weeks, pushing them to nearly 16% at times. 

 Data: Tradeweb; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips Yes, but: CoreWeave, some might say, is a heavily indebted player unrepresentative of the giant hyperscalers who are really driving the boom. 

 That's true. But even the tech behemoths are seeing their borrowing and spending binge start to impinge on their once mighty cash flows. Data: FactSet, company filings; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips What to watch: The continuing rush to the capital markets, with Meta and Microsoft announcing multibillion-dollar offerings just this week. 

 Data: S&P Global Market Intelligence; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips Frightening fact: Massive borrowing binges — especially in the bond market — alongside surging asset prices are one of the few phenomena that academics have found to have a bit of predictive power when it comes to market crashes. 

 The bottom line: We hope these charts don't keep you up at night. 

 Nobody knows when — or if — a crash will hit. 🎃 Happy Halloween! 👻
